title: Learning Rate Annealing Improves Tuning Robustness in Stochastic Optimization
claim: Annealed schedules' convergence coefficients grow sublinearly with misspecification, unlike linear-in-misspecification growth, so they are more robust to coarse tuning.
layout: 1 line plot, coefficient vs misspecification, legend top-left, dashed fitted power-law curves
description: A single line plot with a light dashed grid. The x-axis is the multiplicative stepsize misspecification factor rho, running from about 1 to beyond 20, and the crop cuts the axis label off. The y-axis is the coefficient of the convergence rate, from 4 to 12. A large legend box sits in the upper left. It lists solid curves for cosine annealing (blue), linear decay (green), polynomial decay with p=2 (orange) and p=3 (red). It also lists two dashed reference curves, 5 rho^0.2 (purple) and 4 rho^0.2 (brown). All curves start near 4 to 5 at rho=1 and rise concavely. Linear decay climbs fastest, to about 11. Cosine and p=2 sit in the middle. The p=3 curve is lowest and flattest, and it tracks the 4 rho^0.2 reference. The eye goes first to the legend, then to the diverging solid curves.
caption: Numerically evaluating the coefficient of $\ifrac{\diam \lip}{\sqrt{T}}$ for the convergence guarantee of [ref] with different schedules and varying multiplicative misspecification parameter $\rho$.
abstract: The learning rate in stochastic gradient methods is a critical hyperparameter that is notoriously costly to tune via standard grid search, especially for training modern large-scale models with billions of parameters. We identify a theoretical advantage of learning rate annealing schemes that decay the learning rate to zero at a polynomial rate, such as the widely-used cosine schedule, by demonstrating their increased robustness to initial parameter misspecification due to a coarse grid search. We present an analysis in a stochastic convex optimization setup demonstrating that the convergence rate of stochastic gradient descent with annealed schedules depends sublinearly on the multiplicative misspecification factor $Ï$ (i.e., the grid resolution), achieving a rate of $O(Ï^{1/(2p+1)}/\sqrt{T})$ where $p$ is the degree of polynomial decay and $T$ is the number of steps. This is in contrast to the $O(Ï/\sqrt{T})$ rate obtained under the inverse-square-root and fixed stepsize schedules, which depend linearly on $Ï$. Experiments confirm the increased robustness compared to tuning with a fixed stepsize, that has significant implications for the computational overhead of hyperparameter search in practical training scenarios.
